data.targetWord: American Standard Code for Information Interchange; a 7-bit character encoding standard that represents 128 characters including uppercase and lowercase letters, digits 0–9, punctuation, and control characters.

examples.en-GB: In ASCII, the uppercase letter A is encoded as denary 65 and stored as the binary pattern 1000001.

data.targetWord: A universal character encoding standard that supports over 143,000 characters, covering virtually all world writing systems including Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Hindi, and emoji.

examples.en-GB: Unicode was created to replace ASCII because ASCII could only represent English and a few other Western characters.

data.targetWord: A defined mapping between numbers and characters that a computer system can represent; ASCII and Unicode are two different character sets.

examples.en-GB: The ASCII character set assigns a unique number to each of its 128 characters.

data.targetWord: The smallest single coloured unit in a digital image; short for 'picture element'. An image is made up of a rectangular grid of pixels.

examples.en-GB: When you zoom in to a digital photograph, you can see the individual square pixels that make up the image.

data.targetWord: The number of bits used to represent the colour of a single pixel; more bits means more possible colours and higher image quality, but also a larger file size.

examples.en-GB: A 1-bit colour depth gives 2 colours (black and white); 8-bit gives 256 colours; 24-bit gives about 16.7 million colours.

data.targetWord: Another term for colour depth — the number of bits used to represent the colour of one pixel in a digital image.

examples.en-GB: A bit depth of 24 means 24 bits are used per pixel, allowing approximately 16.7 million different colours.

data.targetWord: The number of pixels in an image, expressed as width × height in pixels; higher resolution means more detail and a sharper image but a larger file.

examples.en-GB: A Full HD image has a resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels, giving approximately 2 million pixels in total.

data.targetWord: The total amount of storage space required by a file; for an uncompressed image it is calculated as width × height × colour depth (in bits), then divided by 8 to convert to bytes.

examples.en-GB: A 100 × 200 pixel image with 8-bit colour depth has a file size of 100 × 200 × 8 ÷ 8 = 20,000 bytes.

data.targetWord: The process of converting data (characters, colours, sounds) into a binary (0s and 1s) representation so that a computer can store and process it.

examples.en-GB: Binary encoding assigns the binary pattern 01000001 to represent the character A in ASCII.

data.targetWord: A single letter, digit, symbol, punctuation mark, or control code that can be stored and represented by a character encoding such as ASCII or Unicode.

examples.en-GB: The characters A, a, 0, space, and ! are all single characters with their own ASCII code numbers.

data.targetWord: A unique numerical value assigned to a character in a character encoding system; for example, the code point for A in ASCII is 65.

examples.en-GB: Every Unicode character has a unique code point; the code point for the emoji smiley face is U+1F600.

data.targetWord: The most common implementation of Unicode; uses variable-length encoding of 1 to 4 bytes per character and is backwards-compatible with ASCII for the first 128 characters.

examples.en-GB: Most web pages use UTF-8 encoding so that text from any language can be displayed correctly in a browser.

data.targetWord: An 8-bit extension of ASCII that encodes 256 characters (2⁸); the first 128 are identical to standard ASCII, and the extra 128 add accented letters and currency symbols for Western European languages.

examples.en-GB: Extended ASCII can represent characters like é, ü, and ñ that standard 7-bit ASCII cannot.

data.targetWord: A colour depth of 24 bits per pixel, using 8 bits each for the red, green, and blue channels, allowing approximately 16.7 million different colours.

examples.en-GB: Digital photographs typically use true colour (24-bit) because the 16.7 million colour options produce smooth, realistic images.

data.targetWord: Red-Green-Blue; the colour model used in digital images where each pixel's colour is defined by the intensity of its red, green, and blue components, each stored as one byte (0–255).

examples.en-GB: The RGB values (255, 0, 0) represent pure red; (0, 255, 0) represents pure green; (255, 255, 255) represents white.

data.targetWord: A digital image format that stores colour information for every individual pixel in a grid; also called a raster image. Bitmap files are uncompressed and typically have large file sizes.

examples.en-GB: A bitmap image stores every pixel's colour, so a 1920×1080 24-bit bitmap takes about 6 MB of storage.

data.targetWord: A digital image that stores data as a grid of pixels; also called a bitmap image. Raster images lose quality when enlarged because you see the individual pixels.

examples.en-GB: JPEG and PNG files are raster images — enlarging them too much results in a blurry, pixelated appearance.

data.targetWord: How detailed and accurate an image appears, determined by both its resolution (number of pixels) and its colour depth (number of bits per pixel); both affect file size.

examples.en-GB: Increasing resolution and colour depth both improve image quality but also increase the file size.

data.targetWord: Data that describes other data; in image files, metadata includes information such as the image dimensions, colour depth, camera settings, and creation date, stored alongside the pixel data.

examples.en-GB: The metadata in a JPEG photo stores the image resolution, date taken, and camera model.

data.targetWord: A group of 8 bits; the standard unit for measuring file sizes and character storage. One byte can store 256 different values (0 to 255).

examples.en-GB: Each character in an ASCII text file occupies exactly one byte of storage.

data.targetWord: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,024 bytes; used to measure small files such as plain text documents.

examples.en-GB: A plain text file with a short paragraph of text might be around 1–2 KB in size.

data.targetWord: A unit of digital storage equal to 1,024 kilobytes; used to measure medium-sized files such as images and audio tracks.

examples.en-GB: An uncompressed true-colour photograph at Full HD resolution takes approximately 6 MB of storage.

data.targetWord: To convert analogue information (such as a physical photograph or a sound wave) into a digital binary representation that a computer can store and process.

examples.en-GB: Scanning a printed photograph digitises it — the scanner converts the image into a grid of pixel values stored as binary.

data.targetWord: Taking measurements of an analogue signal at regular intervals to create a digital representation; a higher sampling rate captures more detail but produces a larger file.

examples.en-GB: Audio sampling measures the sound wave thousands of times per second; CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second.

data.targetWord: A non-printable ASCII character that performs an action rather than displaying a symbol, such as newline (moving to the next line), tab, or carriage return.

examples.en-GB: When you press Enter, a newline control character is inserted into the text file to mark the end of that line.

data.targetWord: The way in which a type of data — text, images, sound, video — is encoded and stored as binary numbers inside a computer.

examples.en-GB: The representation of an image stores each pixel's colour as a binary number using the assigned colour depth.

data.targetWord: A technique for reducing the file size of data by encoding it more efficiently; important for images because uncompressed files are very large.

examples.en-GB: JPEG compression reduces image file sizes significantly, though it may slightly reduce image quality.

data.targetWord: A property of an encoding system where newer data remains readable by systems that only support the older version; UTF-8 is backwards compatible with ASCII.

examples.en-GB: UTF-8 is backwards compatible with ASCII — any ASCII file is valid UTF-8 because the first 128 character codes are identical.

data.title: Calculating Image File Size
data.instruction: Put these steps in the correct order to calculate the file size of an image.
items: Find the resolution of the image (width in pixels × height in pixels)
Find the colour depth of the image in bits per pixel
Multiply: width × height × colour depth to get the file size in bits
Divide by 8 to convert bits to bytes
Divide by 1,024 to convert bytes to kilobytes if needed

data.title: How a Character Is Stored in a Computer
data.instruction: Put these steps in the correct order to describe how a character is stored in computer memory.
items: The user types a character on the keyboard
The operating system looks up the character's code point in the character encoding (e.g. ASCII or Unicode)
The code point number is converted into its binary representation
The binary pattern is stored in RAM as a pattern of bits
When the character needs to be displayed, the binary is decoded back to the character using the same encoding
